column2: Ask HN: Is Agentic Coding really faster?
column3: "I am trying to get a grasp of what we can do with agents. I am an avid user of agentic coding. But somehow I think I code faster by hand (by IDEs I mean). I've always had a sketch approach to coding. Where I kinda lay out the pieces of what needs to be done and then finish them in chunks. That way you keep building a mental picture of what needs doing. Lately I've noticed something - its quite fast to analyze a new code-base with agents for sure especially messy ones. But once I do get a hold of the codebase (even larger ones)
column4: I can change things by hand quite quickly. My bottleneck seems to be typing
column5: but manipulating the mental map is a lot faster. Does this match other folks experience or am I deluding myself ?"

column3: I was thinking about how Advent Of Code and how coding has changed. I think it could be a good way to also teach and explore prompting styles with a specific objective in mind. Does anything like this exist or does it sound interesting for someone to build? column2: Ask HN: Frontier Capability on Average Computers
column3: "I really want to find a way to get frontier-level intelligence on local hardware. I think some really cool ways to get this have been done already like the technique of spreading an LLMs weights across a fast-enough SSD and then only serving up an expert at a time on the GPU/SoC. I have this idea to make a tool that lets people download several small open-weight models and they act like experts but are different very task specific models with a harness designed to keep track of their thoughts & work to let normal hardware be able to get close to frontier (or just useful level intelligence). Basically
column4: I want to have a model that acts like a router or decision maker where you start your chat with initially (say a coding task for example) and it decides what model does the work next. If it needs to research it writes down in an .MD what it needs to find out
column5: if it needs to write code
column6: another model starts working but the other models memory & work get saved to an .MD (or folder of .MDs) and lets you get real work done but completely locally. This might already be done but its just an idea I had and I wanted to see what the smart people on the internet thought or how they would approach this. I might also just be able to ask AI."

column2: Ask HN: Are signed URL previews feasible?
column3: "Lots of protocols and software allow URL previews. But they have some annoying limitations: For centralized public services the server can just retrieve the preview and serve it. But for decentralized services like Mastodon either every server has to fetch the preview on its own leading to lots of traffic and potential discrepancies between the previews served by different servers or the origin home server sends the preview but now everyone has to trust that it is authentic. The home server to which a link gets posted could place anything as its preview and thereby indirectly impersonate the URL and fake its content. For E2EE messengers things are even more annoying because you do not want the servers to see the URL at all. So either all parties have to retrieve the preview on their own meaning they have to connect to a random
column4: potentially malicious URL or only the sender does and everyone has to trust the sender that the preview is authentic which is a great opportunity for scams.^1 The perfect solution would be a standard for web servers to sign URL previews with their CA issued certificate. So that you can always proof that a preview is authentic. RFC 9421 already standardizes this. But this will not happen. There is virtually no chance of widespread adoption. So my idea is: You retrieve a webpage and record the whole TLS session including certificates
column5: MACs and your key material like nonce and client random from the handshake. Now you use this as the basis for the URL preview. When you include your secret material from the TLS handshake anyone should be able to verify that the content is authentic from the server serving the URL due to the CA certificate and authentication of TLS traffic. Standardize the request headers and limit the response length. Just cut off everything after the limit. Define some algorithm for computing the preview that ever recipient can verify. If you want to include linked images in the preview that increases complexity but should be doable. Repeat the whole thing with the linked image and create a bundle from all requests that authenticates the preview. The downside I see is complexity and the need for the receiver to parse the preview bundle which might be attack surface. Does anything similar already exist? Am I missing something or do you think this might be feasible to implement? [1] Many messengers solve this by providing a URL preview service on the server. The client sends the URL to the messenger service which retrieves (and signs I hope) a URL preview which the client then includes in the message. This has the advantage that none of the parties of the conversation has to directly connect to an untrusted UTL. This bypasses E2EE for URLs. You can usually opt of this by disabling previews. Consider this if you did not know about this."

column2: Ask HN: What Happened in DNSSEC Yesterday?
column3: "I have had DNSSEC verification enabled for a couple of months in systemd-resolved. Not that I am particular paranoid or do any nuclear-sensitive stuff on my machine. Don't even own any Bitcoin. But mostly out of technical curiosity. Until yesterday I had only noticed 2 broken sites (or sites affected by buggy systemd-resolved implementation as some voices claim). Some Jira Plugin and Swedish Railways SJ. Yesterday basically the Internet stopped working for me. After a while I remembered good old operator wisdom ""It's always DNS"". And it was DNS. Systemd-resolved logged ""missing-key"" for basically every query I tried. So I switched from DoT 1.1.1.1 @Cloudflare to DoT 8.8.8.8 @Google and life continued. Until today that suddenly out of nowhere showed the same symptom. Turning off DNSSEC verification avoids the problem. An internet search brought up https://github.com/NordSecurity/nordvpn-linux/issues/1853 which also links to another one. The timing seems to match with my observation
column4: but I don't use NordVPN. Any clues?"

column8: then transitioned to how modern America's civil rights crimes are perpetrated against those who can't afford an expensive attorney to represent them. column2: Ask HN: Is this the beginning of the end of open source?
column3: "If you're following the photopea incident
column4: I'm sure you'd concur that the writing was on the wall. It's an inevitable outcome of the rise of AI in software dev. Any project that sees a semblance of success will be cloned overnight many times over and will find itself competing with its own copies. We saw glimpses of a similar situation in the past when large cloud platforms cloned popular softwares in a not a very dissimilar manner. This led to the creation of ""source available"" as an alternative to open source that gained some traction of its own. But since this mostly affected a few large players
column5: open source by and itself was large unaffected still supported by large volumes of individuals driven by passion
column6: motivated towards their craft. The concept of open source is itself something of an anomaly not seen in any other industry or at any other time in history. Partly fueled by an individual's desire to exhibit original work
column7: and partly supported by the fact that code needs someone of an equal to work with
column8: it still allowed authors to reap a net benefit while giving out their IP for free. LLMs have turned that picture over completely. It's not only trivial to derive
column9: for all purposes
column10: an exact copy of the IP while obscuring the source
column11: it's also possible to maintain and operate the IP with a relatively low bar of expertise. But the other inconspicuous problem brought about by LLMs is that can you even claim original work any more? When no one believes that you wrote it yourself
column12: what motivation remains to continue publishing as open source? With no net benefit to revealing your IP
column13: will we see a revival to closed source distribution again?"
